chapters.title: Elders and the defence of sound teaching

parts.text: Paul greets Titus as his son in their shared faith, grounding his ministry in the truth that produces godliness and God’s promise of eternal life. Titus remains in Crete to complete unfinished matters and appoint elders in every city. Leaders must be blameless husbands of one wife, with faithful and orderly children. As God’s stewards, they should avoid arrogance, anger, violence, drunkenness, and greed, while practicing hospitality, goodness, and self-control. They must hold sound teaching to encourage believers and answer opponents.

Many rebellious deceivers, especially of the circumcision, upset entire households for dishonest gain. Titus must rebuke them sharply so they become sound in faith, turning away from Jewish fables and human commands that reject truth. Paul contrasts the pure with people whose minds and consciences are defiled. Their claim to know God is contradicted by disobedient works and unfitness for good service.

Titus must teach conduct fitting sound doctrine. Older men should be sober and steadfast in faith, love, and patience; older women should live reverently and teach younger women faithful family conduct and purity. Young men need self-control, while Titus must model good works and trustworthy teaching that gives opponents no valid accusation. Servants should obey honestly and faithfully, making the teaching of God attractive through their conduct.

God’s saving grace teaches believers to reject ungodliness and worldly desires and live uprightly in the present world. They await the blessed hope and glorious appearing of the great God and Saviour Jesus Christ. He gave himself to redeem them from iniquity and purify a people belonging to him, eager for good works. Titus must declare, encourage, and correct with authority rather than allow his ministry to be disregarded.

Believers should obey authorities, be ready for good works, avoid slander and quarrels, and treat everyone gently. Paul recalls that they too once lived foolishly, enslaved to desires and mutual hatred. God’s kindness and love saved them through mercy, not their righteous deeds, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Ghost richly given through Jesus. Justified by grace, they become heirs of eternal life’s hope. Titus must affirm these truths so believers devote themselves to useful good works.

Foolish disputes, genealogies, and arguments about the law are unprofitable and should be avoided. A divisive heretic who refuses repeated correction must be rejected. Paul gives travel instructions, asks Titus to join him at Nicopolis, and directs assistance for Zenas and Apollos. The believers should learn productive service that meets real needs. He closes with greetings and grace.
